<p>\"We have pet care experience\" is no:

<p>A cat that smells a day or two after:
A cat that smells a day or two after a bath is almost always damp rather than dirty. Moisture trapped at the skin creates conditions for bacterial growth, and the result is an unpleasant smell that no product applied to the coat will fix, because the problem is under the coat rather than in it.

Towel-drying lifts the surface water and does little else. The coat underneath stays wet. Drying has to reach the skin: a hairdryer on a low setting, kept moving, until the coat feels dry all the way through rather than just to the hand on top. For a long-haired cat this takes longer than most people expect.
<p>A distributor ordering by the carton:
A distributor ordering by the carton is making a different decision from a salon ordering for itself, and the useful comparison is not price per bottle. It is how much volume each format moves, how many SKUs you can carry on one pallet, and how many of them make a health claim.

This page sets out the ordering framework. Every commercial figure — minimum order, price, production time — is confirmed against your specific enquiry once the destination and quantity are known.
<p>A full bath is required when the coat:
A full bath is required when the coat is genuinely soiled — fecal contamination, mud through the coat, urine staining, or a double coat that has not been washed in long enough to have collected its own oil and debris. None of that is a spot clean, and no foam substitutes for it.

A wet shampoo is also the only route to conditioning a long or double coat, because the rinse is what removes the loosened dead hair and the residue. Silk protein in a 500 mL shampoo conditions the hair shaft; it needs water to do that.
<p>A gate is a requirement that must be:
A gate is a requirement that must be satisfied before detailed comparison is worthwhile. There are seven worth testing, and the sequence is deliberate — a supplier that fails the first one does not need the other six answered.

1. Can it make the format? Not "do you do pet care" but the specific format: a 500 mL shampoo with a flip-top and a 300 mL foam with a specific pump. Ask which similar formats it has produced and in what quantities.

2. Can it support the route you need? Stock formula with your label, or a new formula developed for you. These are different products with different timelines, and a supplier offering both will tell you which one you are getting.

3. Can the proposed package work with the product? A viscous shampoo and a thin spray do not want the same closure. Ask whether the pack has been reviewed against the formula's viscosity, not just chosen from a catalogue.

4. Is the sample and approval process usable? How many rounds, what each round costs, how long each takes, and who holds the approved version.

5. Are the quotation inclusions visible? Formula, filling, packaging, printing, testing, documents, inspection, freight. Eight lines. A single figure without its exclusions is not a quotation.

6. Can the claims be verified? The certificate, the site, the standard, the scope, the dates, and the route to verify. If the answer is a brochure, the gate has not been passed.

7. Can responsibilities be confirmed before production? Who owns the artwork, who approves the final specification, who signs off the shipment, and what happens when a batch does not match.

A supplier that fails a project-critical gate should leave the shortlist, regardless of what it quoted. This is uncomfortable to do with a factory that answered your questions in an hour, and it is exactly the case where the saved time turns into a wasted order.
<p>A healthy adult cat that grooms itsel:
A healthy adult cat that grooms itself does not need bathing. This is not a preference; a cat's own grooming removes loose hair and distributes the oils that keep the coat conditioned, and washing that off leaves the coat dull and the skin more prone to irritation. Cats that are bathed on a schedule tend to need it more.

A bath is warranted in a short list of situations:

After a flea or topical treatment, because the product has to reach the skin rather than sit on the coat. After an episode that soiled the coat, particularly diarrhoea, where the coat is genuinely contaminated. When a long-haired or show cat cannot groom an area itself — mats behind the ears and in the armpits are the places a cat physically cannot reach.

Everything else on the list of reasons to bathe a cat is usually a grooming problem or a dirt problem, and both are better solved without water.
<p>A manufacturer suited to an establish:
A manufacturer suited to an established shampoo formula may not fit a fine-mist spray, a foam cleanser, a paw gel or a multi-SKU retail line. The formats differ in viscosity, in how they dispense, in what they need from a closure, and in what they do to a label. Comparing quotes that answered different projects is how a buyer ends up with a number that cannot be delivered.

Give every supplier the same written brief, and make it specific enough that two different suppliers would quote the same thing:

— the target market and the main sales channel
— the product type and its intended use
— the formula starting point, whether you bring one or want one developed
— the packaging and dispensing direction, including the closure and the artwork language
— the estimated quantity per SKU, and whether it is a first run or a reorder
— the sample and review process you expect
— the documents or evidence you need
— the target launch window, and which date in it is fixed

Then add a line for what is still open. A brief that admits two unresolved questions is more useful than one that pretends the project is fully defined, because the suppliers who can answer those questions are the ones worth talking to.
<p>A no-rinse foam removes three of the:
A no-rinse foam removes three of the four expensive parts of a bath: filling a tub, waiting for a rinse, and drying. It is applied, worked in and left. For an animal too stressed for handling, or a kennel line where throughput matters more than presentation, that is the difference between a five-minute job and a thirty-minute one.

Two sizes suit different animals. The 500 mL is for larger dogs and for a full spot clean; the 300 mL is the practical size for cats and small breeds. A dedicated 200 mL paw format exists for animals coming in from outside, where the paws are the part that actually needs attention.
<p>A pet shampoo is a surfactant in a bo: A pet shampoo is a surfactant in a bottle, and almost everything that determines whether it is gentle comes down to four things: which surfactant, what the pH is, what else is in the water, and whether it actually rinses out. A buyer who asks four questions gets a better answer than one who reads twenty marketing claims. Here are seven, in the order they matter.
<p>A red flag is not an automatic reject:
A red flag is not an automatic rejection. It is a reason to ask one more question and weight the answer.

1. The supplier confirms everything without asking about the project.
2. It cannot explain experience with your specific format.
3. It gives a minimum order or a lead time without defining the scope.
4. It provides certificates that cannot be connected to the actual site.
5. It lists documents without explaining what they cover.
6. It treats formula and packaging as two separate decisions.
7. It provides samples with no version control.
8. It leaves major quotation exclusions unclear.
9. It avoids explaining which work is outsourced.
10. It presents document review or market review as a guaranteed approval.

Number ten deserves particular attention in pet care, because it is common and it is expensive. A manufacturer can support a claim with test data; it cannot authorise that claim for your market. A supplier who says your wording will be approved is describing a process they do not control. If a claim matters to your business, budget for your own substantiation before you launch, not after a complaint.
<p>A room where the cat is clean can sti:
A room where the cat is clean can still smell of cat, and the reason is usually the blanket, the towel or the cat bed rather than the animal. Bedding holds the residue that a coat sheds over time, and ordinary laundry detergent is built for fabric and general soil rather than for organic residue.

A detergent formulated with biological enzymes does a different job. Enzymes break down the specific organic compounds that produce the smell, rather than merely suspending them in water and leaving them in the fabric. This is the same principle as the litter deodorizer, applied to textiles instead of to litter.

The practical habit is to wash cat bedding hot and to wash it more often than feels necessary. A blanket that is washed monthly can hold a build-up that a single wash does not clear, because the residue has had a month to accumulate.
<p>A salon does not buy shampoo the way:
A salon does not buy shampoo the way a household does. A household buys one bottle and wants it to be good. A salon buys by the carton, repeats the order every few weeks, and its cost per bath is decided by two numbers that rarely appear on a product page: how many bottles are in a carton, and what that carton weighs.

This page covers what a salon, a mobile groomer or a distributor needs to evaluate a supplier — the commercial figures are confirmed against your enquiry, but the framework is stated here so you can ask the right questions.
<p>A shampoo and a wash are not the same:
A shampoo and a wash are not the same product. A shampoo is a surfactant you work through and rinse. A wash is the broader category, which may be a liquid, a foam, or a no-rinse format for spot cleaning. Comparing a 1.5 kg liquid bottle against a 200 mL foam pump on price per millilitre is comparing two different jobs.

Decide the job first — full bath, spot clean, or coat conditioning — then compare within that job.
<p>A supplier that treats these as three:
A supplier that treats these as three separate conversations is telling you they will be three separate problems later. The chain runs: formula properties → dispensing → closure → sealing or leakage → artwork space → packing and shipping → what the end user actually experiences.

Five questions reveal whether the chain is managed or merely assembled:

— How is packaging reviewed against the formula's viscosity and application?
— How are stock components, special-order components and custom components distinguished?
— Are approved formula and package versions recorded, or just remembered?
— How are samples identified, and how is buyer feedback tracked against them?
— What are the limits, the fees and the timing effects of a revision?

One caveat worth keeping: a good first sample is useful evidence, and it is not proof. Sample feel, appearance, scent and performance need their own evaluation process, separate from the supplier conversation. And the gap between a 50 mL sample and a 24,000-bottle run is exactly where packaging problems appear.
<p>A technically capable manufacturer ca:
A technically capable manufacturer can still be a poor commercial fit, and the difference is nearly always in the scope rather than the number. Confirm each of these before comparing any two quotations:

— the minimum order basis: by formula, fragrance, size, package, artwork, or per SKU
— what happens to unused packaging and printed material
— sample rounds and any development charges
— the condition that starts production, and the condition that pauses it
— the quoted timeline, and which stages it excludes
— inclusions: formula, filling, packaging, printing, testing, documents, inspection, freight
— payment terms, and how long the quotation stays valid
— reorder minimums, component continuity, and the storage conditions for retained material
— ownership of artwork, tooling, specifications and buyer-supplied information

A cost that remains pending when the scope is incomplete should be labelled pending. A supplier that presents an assumption as a settled price is asking you to find the difference later, usually in the worst month of the project.

On the minimum order itself, note what it is calculated on. A minimum stated as a unit count and a minimum stated per SKU are different commitments, and a supplier with a 1,000-unit minimum on two SKUs is not offering the same thing as one with 2,000 bottles on one SKU. Ask which basis applies, and what happens to the second SKU.
<p>A waterless cleansing foam is a mild:
A waterless cleansing foam is a mild surfactant in a foam format that is applied, worked in, wiped or towel-dried, and left. It does not need water and it does not need rinsing. That is the whole of the proposition, and it is a genuinely useful one — for paws after a walk, for a patch of dirt, for a travelling animal, and for any animal whose stress around bathing is worse than the dirt.

It is also, precisely, a spot clean. Applied to a matted coat or a fecal soiling, it will not do the job.
<p>Ask for a range, not a number. Pet sk:
Ask for a range, not a number. Pet skin sits close to mildly acidic, and a surfactant system that performs across roughly 5.5 to 7 suits regular bathing. A supplier who quotes a single pH to two decimal places has measured one sample, not the product.

This is also a fast way to tell whether you are talking to a formulator or a reseller. It takes one sentence to answer, and the answer is either specific or it is vague.
<p>At minimum: a batch certificate of an:
At minimum: a batch certificate of analysis, a safety data sheet, the commercial invoice with the HS code, and a certificate of origin. The HS code matters more than it looks — the grooming line in this catalogue sits under 3307.10 for soaps, 3307.90 for other preparations and 3402.20 for detergents, and getting the classification right at the outset avoids a customs query at the border.

If you are buying for resale rather than for your own animals, ask whether the manufacturer publishes its third-party laboratory determinations and whether you may cite them. A supplier who will not show the report is telling you something.
<p>Blankets, bedding and towels in a she:
Blankets, bedding and towels in a shelter carry the same odor as the animals, and they are frequently the reason a kennel smells even after cleaning. A detergent formulated for pet hair and pet odor, built on biological enzymes rather than ordinary surfactants, is a 1.5 kg bottle at 6 per carton.

It is a heavier carton than anything else in the range at 10.5 kg, which makes it worth including in a mixed order alongside lighter cartons so the pallet fills evenly.
<p>Carton density varies enormously acro:
Carton density varies enormously across this line — from 2.5 kg for the paw gel to 10.5 kg for the laundry detergent — and that variation decides whether your freight quote lands well. A mixed order that pairs a heavy carton with a light one fills a pallet better than a single-SKU order of the same total volume, and freight is per pallet before it is per bottle.

Practical pairings: the 1.5 kg detergent carton with the 200 mL wash or the paw foam; the 100 mL ear cleanser carton with the 300 mL foam. Ask for the pallet plan before you commit — it is a five-minute question that can change the landed cost materially.
<p>Choosing a pet care manufacturer in C:
Choosing a pet care manufacturer in China is usually presented as a comparison: five quotations side by side, a spreadsheet of unit prices, and a certificate list from each. That approach fails in a specific way — it rewards the supplier who answers quickly and completely the question you asked, rather than the supplier who can do the work.

This page is the order of operations. It is written for a brand owner, a distributor or a regional importer who is shortlisting factories, and it is deliberately structured so that the disqualifying questions come before the comparing ones. A supplier that fails a project-critical gate should not remain a candidate because it quoted the lowest price or replied fastest — that is the single most expensive mistake in this process, and it is made by buyers who were told to compare first.

Nothing here is veterinary advice, legal advice, or a market approval. It is a framework for supplier evaluation and the questions worth asking before you spend money on samples.

<p>Cleaning and conditioning are cosmeti:
Cleaning and conditioning are cosmetic claims. Antibacterial, antifungal and mite-control are health claims, and in most markets they bring the product into the biocide regulatory frame, which means a production licence and supporting laboratory data.

This matters commercially, not just legally. If you are importing into the EU or the US, a product making a biocidal claim is classified differently from one that does not, and the classification follows the claim on the label. If a supplier is vague about which frame their product sits in, that is a question to resolve before you order rather than after.
<p>Cocamidopropyl betaine, a coconut-der:
Cocamidopropyl betaine, a coconut-derived surfactant, is the mildest of the commonly available and is what you want to see first for a regular bathing product. It cleans adequately and does not strip the coat.

Sodium lauryl sulfate cleans harder and foams more. It is not dangerous on pet skin, but it is a drying choice, and on a double-coated breed or a frequent-bathing animal it shows. Sodium laureth sulfate is the milder variant of the same family and sits between the two.

The practical rule: a product whose main surfactant is a sulfate is a cleansing-forward formula, and one built on a betaine is a daily-use formula. Neither is wrong; they are different products.
<p>Do not ask whether the factory makes:
Do not ask whether the factory makes high-quality products. Ask what evidence applies to the legal entity, the manufacturing site, the process, the product and the batch. These are five different things, and a supplier can have good evidence for two of them.

Company and site. The legal company name, the manufacturing-site name and address, which entity appears on the quotation and the contract, which site fills the product, and which operations are outsourced. A quotation from one entity and production in another is a real arrangement, and it is a legitimate one — as long as you know.

Certificates. For any certificate, check the facility name and address, the standard it cites, its scope, the issuing organisation, the issue and expiry dates, the verification route, and whether the scope reaches the site that will make your product. This is the check most often skipped. A facility certificate covers a site and a standard. It is not an approval of a product, and it does not transfer to a second site under the same company.

Process and batch. The evidence worth asking about is the machinery that turns an approved formula into an identifiable finished batch: incoming material checks, batch records, in-process controls, filling and packaging checks, batch or date coding, traceability, finished-product inspection, retained samples, deviation handling and change control.

The objective of this step is narrow and concrete: understand how an approved formula and package become a batch you can name, find and document six months from now.
<p>Even with daily scooping, urine passe:
Even with daily scooping, urine passes through the litter and reaches the bottom of the box, where it soaks into the base and the litter beneath the surface layer. What you cannot see is what has already soaked through.

Ammonia is what makes urine smell sharp. It is produced as urea breaks down, and it rises as a gas. This is why a box that looks clean can still smell strongly — the visible layer is new, and the odor is coming from underneath it.

Most odor-control products address the smell you can smell. The ones that work address the ammonia itself.
For a home buyer this barely matters. For anyone ordering by the carton it is the number that decides the freight bill. Bottle or sachet count per carton, carton dimensions and gross weight are worth asking for up front, because a 12-bottle carton and a 24-bottle carton of the same product are not the same landed cost.

Sachets are the other format worth knowing: a 10 g sachet ships 100 to a carton and needs no secondary packaging, which is why sachets are the usual choice for sample packs and for products added to an existing routine.
<p>For each SKU: bottles per carton, gro:
For each SKU: bottles per carton, gross carton weight, carton dimensions, HS code, and shelf life. Across the grooming line the HS codes are 3307.10 for the soaps and shampoos, 3307.90 for the ear cleanser and paw gel, and 3402.20 for the detergent — so three classifications cover eleven products, and getting them right at the outset avoids a customs query.

Then confirm the commercial terms for the order as a whole: the minimum that applies to a mixed order, the price at your volume, the production time, and the delivery basis once the destination is agreed. Freight and duty are quoted separately from the product price, so the landed figure stays unambiguous.
<p>Four documents, every shipment:</p><p:
Four documents, every shipment:

A batch certificate of analysis, specific to the lot, not a generic one. A 16-language safety data sheet. The commercial invoice with the HS code on it. A certificate of origin.

For any product making a biocidal claim — antibacterial, antifungal, mite control — ask whether the manufacturer publishes its third-party laboratory determinations and whether you may cite them in your own marketing. If the answer is no, plan your own substantiation before you launch rather than after a complaint.
<p>If you are building a salon-owned bra:
If you are building a salon-owned brand, private label covers bottle, label, box and colour, with EN and Chinese label compliance for the destination market. The formula can be ours or developed for you.

The two variables that change the timeline are worth asking about early: whether the formula is new, and whether the label artwork is new. Both add time before the filling run can be scheduled. Production time and cost for a private-label programme are confirmed against the specific brief.
<p>Ingredients like nano silver ions, ch:
Ingredients like nano silver ions, chlorine dioxide or plant extracts used against mites are a different category. They make the product a treatment rather than a cosmetic, and in most jurisdictions that brings it into a regulated frame requiring production licensing and supporting laboratory data.

This has a practical consequence for anyone buying to resell: the claim on the label determines the regulatory classification at import. A shampoo that says it controls mites and one that says it cleanses are, from a customs and compliance point of view, different products even if the base formula is similar.
<p>Intake animals arrive with more than:
Intake animals arrive with more than surface dirt. Mud, fecal soiling and urine staining need a proper wash, and this is where a liquid shampoo earns its place. The multi-purpose wash is the general-purpose format — mild betaine base with camellia seed extract — and the 300 mL and 200 mL sizes cover everything from small dogs to larger animals without a bulk bottle.

The 200 mL size ships 24 to a carton, which makes it the highest-density carton in the washing range at 5.5 kg, which is worth knowing when freight is the deciding cost.
<p>Intake washing is a different problem:
Intake washing is a different problem from home bathing. The constraint is not the animal's coat — it is staff time. A shelter processing twenty arrivals a week does not need a luxury bath; it needs the shortest procedure that leaves the animal clean and the volunteer unoccupied for half an hour.

This page covers the formats that suit that situation, and is written for shelters, rescues and the distributors who serve them.
<p>Keep both away from eyes and ears, an:
Keep both away from eyes and ears, and do not use any of them on broken or inflamed skin without advice. A foam applied to a hot, weeping patch is not treating the patch, and it can make the situation worse.

For skin that is actively irritated, the right next step is a vet. No shampoo in this range replaces one.
<p>Litter box odor comes from urine resi: Litter box odor comes from urine residue, not the litter itself. Urine breaks down into ammonia over 24–72 hours, and that ammonia rising off the surface is what you smell. Ventilation helps a little, but ventilation cannot remove a smell that is still being produced. It has to be stopped at the source.
<p>Mild surfactant, stated pH range, sho:
Mild surfactant, stated pH range, short readable ingredient list, a claim you can classify, the format your animals actually need, and the carton figures. A supplier who answers all six clearly is manufacturing; one who answers with adjectives is reselling.

Every figure on a product page — the minimum order, the production time, the price — is confirmed against your enquiry once the destination and the quantity are known.
<p>Odor control is a litter problem. If:
Odor control is a litter problem. If the behaviour has changed, it is not. See a vet if you notice:

  • Blood in the urine, or litter that clumps hard in the box rather than in the tray
  • A sudden change in how often your cat urinates, or straining to urinate
  • A cat that has started avoiding the box entirely
  • Unusual thirst or changes in drinking

Urinary obstruction is an emergency in cats and is easily mistaken for a litter-box problem. If straining produces nothing, that is a vet visit the same day.
<p>Only score suppliers that cleared the:
Only score suppliers that cleared the gates. Scoring a supplier that cannot make your format is a way of making a bad fit look better than a good one.

Product and route fit — 20%
Formula and packaging fit — 20%
Quality and evidence fit — 20%
Sampling and change control — 15%
Commercial and operational fit — 15%
Communication and responsibility fit — 10%

Grade each on a five-point scale, and write the evidence and the open question next to the number:

1 — Poor fit. 2 — Significant gaps. 3 — Possible fit with open questions. 4 — Strong fit with usable evidence. 5 — Strong fit with clear evidence and responsibilities.

Multiply each weight by the grade over five, then add. Grades of 4, 4, 3, 5, 3 and 4 give 16 + 16 + 12 + 15 + 9 + 8 = 76 out of 100.

One rule matters more than the weights: do not calculate a passing score for a supplier that failed a critical gate or lacks evidence for a project-critical decision. Mark that supplier Hold — not scored until the gap is resolved. A number compares fit among eligible suppliers. It does not verify a certificate, it does not prove product suitability, and it cannot cancel an unresolved critical risk.
<p>Perfume in a pet shampoo is a human p:
Perfume in a pet shampoo is a human preference. It does nothing for the animal and it is the component most often implicated in a cat refusing to be bathed — not because the smell is offensive to the cat, but because a heavily scented animal is a stressed animal.

One practical caution: fragrance usually appears at the end of the ingredient list regardless of how much is present, because regulations require listing in descending order by weight and fragrance is often added after the main surfactants at a small percentage. A last-position fragrance does not mean a trace amount.
<p>Perfumed litter masks ammonia for a f:
Perfumed litter masks ammonia for a few minutes and can make the problem harder to judge, because the real odor returns once the fragrance fades. Household bleach destroys ammonia by reaction, which works, but it is a caustic: it damages litter, irritates paws, and leaves a residue you then have to rinse out completely.

Neither approach addresses what is producing the smell.
<p>Read the first ingredient. If it is a:
Read the first ingredient. If it is a betaine, you are looking at a daily-use formula. Scan for fragrance and for tea tree or citrus, and if either is present, check which species the product is intended for. Everything after that is trade-off you can live with.

The full specification, the ingredient list and the available pack sizes for each product are on its product page. Minimum order, price and production time are confirmed once the destination and quantity are known.
<p>Reading a pet shampoo label takes abo: Reading a pet shampoo label takes about thirty seconds once you know the three things worth checking. Everything else on the list is either unremarkable or a trade-off you can live with. The three are: the surfactant, the fragrance, and the essential oils.
<p>Reply speed is worth something, and i:
Reply speed is worth something, and it is worth much less than it feels like at the point where a supplier answers you in four minutes. What predicts a project going well is whether the supplier says things that are specific enough to be useful.

The distinction is easy to recognise once you see it side by side:

A weak answer is "Yes, we can do it." A strong answer is "We would start from our 500 mL base, change the fragrance to your specification, use a flip-top closure from stock, and quote the artwork separately." The first can be given by anyone. The second is evidence.

Apply the same test to every answer you get. A quote of "MOQ is 2,000" should be followed by what the 2,000 applies to. A lead time of "30 days" should be followed by what the clock starts from and what it excludes. "Documents are available" should be followed by which record, issued by whom, when, and covering what. "Packaging is no problem" should be followed by how the closure, the leakage risk and the sourcing were reviewed.

A supplier that pauses to check a pump, a document, a wording request or a production condition is more dependable than one that agrees to everything immediately. The second supplier is not being accommodating — they are not checking, and the check is what the buyer cannot do for them.

<p>Some SKUs in this line make a health:
Some SKUs in this line make a health claim and some do not. The multi-purpose wash carries nano silver ions; the antibacterial shampoo targets mites and bacterial infection. Both therefore sit inside a regulated frame that a plain shampoo does not, which affects classification, documentation and what you may claim in your own marketing.

For a distributor this is the single most important question to resolve early, because the claim determines what you can print. Decide which SKUs carry a claim and substantiate them properly, or plan the range around the cosmetic formats and treat the claim-bearing ones as a separate line with its own documentation.
<p>Some animals arrive with a skin condi:
Some animals arrive with a skin condition. That is a veterinary matter, not a grooming one, and the distinction matters for a shelter because treatment claims are regulated in most markets and must be substantiated.

The practical rule for an intake line: use a cosmetic wash as the default, and keep a claim-bearing product on the shelf for an animal a vet has already assessed. Buying the treatment format for every animal wastes money and creates a documentation problem.
<p>Take a 500 mL shampoo. A carton holds:
Take a 500 mL shampoo. A carton holds 12 bottles and weighs 8 kg. A 300 mL bottle in the same family ships 12 per carton at 6.8 kg, and a 200 mL bottle ships 24 per carton at 5.5 kg.

Work out the cost per bath before comparing anything. A 500 mL bottle used for one large dog produces roughly two baths; a 300 mL bottle used for one medium dog produces one. The 200 mL format, despite being the smallest per unit, often has the lowest cost per bath in the range, because the carton carries twice the bottle count at a lower gross weight — which is what determines your freight bill.

This is the arithmetic that decides whether a supplier is cheap or expensive for you, and it takes two minutes with the carton figures.
<p>Tea tree oil and citrus oils are the:
Tea tree oil and citrus oils are the two most commonly raised concerns in pet shampoos, and cats are the animals most often reported to react to them. This is not a regulatory restriction so much as a practical one: many cats, particularly young ones, do not metabolise these compounds well.

The rule that follows is simple. A formula with tea tree or citrus belongs on a dog product unless the label says otherwise for cats. It is worth asking a supplier directly whether a given formula is cat-rated, because the answer determines which animals it can be sold for.
<p>The formats here run 500 mL, 300 mL a:
The formats here run 500 mL, 300 mL and a dedicated 200 mL paw size, and the choice is mostly about how much of the animal you are treating.

The 500 mL suits a larger dog or a fuller spot clean. The 300 mL suits cats and small breeds and is the general-purpose travel size. The 200 mL paw format is small enough to carry on a walk and sized for the job it is named after.

For a business buying by the carton, the density differs sharply: twelve per carton at 7.5 kg for the 500 mL, twelve at 5.5 kg for the 300 mL, and twenty-four at 5.5 kg for the paw format. Those figures decide the freight bill.
<p>The resistance is about the process,:
The resistance is about the process, not the product. Four things change the outcome more than any shampoo:

Brush first. A matted coat cannot be washed — the mats hold water against the skin and dry slowly, which causes the exact skin problems the bath was meant to prevent. Remove mats before water goes anywhere near the cat. Use lukewarm water and a non-slip surface. A cat that loses its footing panics, and a cat in a laundry sink is not gripping. Keep it short. A five-minute wash is enough. A long one is what turns a bath into a memory. Dry properly, all the way through. This is the step most often skipped and it is the step that matters most.

The standard minimum is 2,000 bottles per SKU, which is more than a single shelter absorbs in a year. <p>The surfactant does the cleaning, and:
The surfactant does the cleaning, and it is also what determines how much a pet will tolerate. Cocoamide or cocamidopropyl betaine — both coconut-derived — are among the mildest widely available, which is why they appear in nearly every gentle pet shampoo. Sodium lauryl sulfate cleans harder and foams more, and it is the ingredient most often associated with the tight, stripped feeling a human gets from a strong shampoo; on pet skin the concern is dryness rather than a dramatic reaction.

Ask which surfactant the formula is built on. A supplier who names one is a manufacturer; a supplier who says it is a blend without naming the base is buying from a blender.
<p>These are the ingredients that earn t:
These are the ingredients that earn their place in a gentle formula, and they are all conditioning agents rather than active ones:

Camellia seed extract — a light emollient, used across the grooming line in this catalogue for both washing and foaming formats. Silk protein — binds to the hair shaft and is what gives a 500 mL shampoo its conditioning character. Aloe vera extract — in the paw moisturising gel, where the application is genuinely dry and cracked skin. Biological enzymes — in the laundry detergent, where the job is breaking down organic residue in fabric rather than on skin.
<p>This is the question that separates a:
This is the question that separates a dog product from a cat product. Tea tree oil and citrus oils are the two most commonly cited sensitivities, and cats are the animals most often reported to react to them. A formula containing low-concentration tea tree oil belongs on a dog product unless the manufacturer states that it is intended for cats too.

Beyond oils, the ingredients to look for are camellia seed extract, silk protein and aloe — conditioning agents rather than active ones. What you are looking for is a short list you can read, not a paragraph of unpronounceables.
<p>Three things cover most of it, and no:
Three things cover most of it, and none of them needs to be used on a schedule:

A mild wash for the rare real bath. A no-rinse foam for spot cleaning and for cats that will not tolerate a bath. And a detergent formulated for pet bedding and clothing for the things the cat sleeps on, which is the item most households do not buy and then notice the absence of.

<p>Two separate questions usually get se:
Two separate questions usually get searched as one: how do you bathe a cat, and how do you clean the things the cat sleeps on. They have almost nothing in common in practice, and the second one solves a smell that the first one cannot.

This page covers both, including the case where the answer to the first is that you should not bathe the cat at all.
<p>Use a product formulated for cats and:
Use a product formulated for cats and dogs — a mild coconut-derived surfactant base, and nothing heavily fragranced. The mistake is using a dog shampoo on a cat. Dog products are frequently more heavily scented, and cats are the animals most likely to react to strong fragrance and to essential oils such as tea tree and citrus.

For a cat that cannot tolerate a bath, a no-rinse foam removes most of the objection: no tub, no rinsing, minimal drying. It is a spot clean rather than a full bath, so it suits a dirty patch, a matted area a cat cannot reach, or a cat too stressed for the full procedure.
<p>Use a staged process: define the proj:
Use a staged process: define the project, build a longlist, apply the gates, send the same brief to the suppliers that passed, review the evidence, compare samples and terms, complete the scorecard, select a preferred supplier, and confirm the pre-production scope in writing.

— the product and market scope
— the manufacturing route and the formula route
— the approved sample and its specification
— the packaging and artwork versions
— the minimum order and the quotation scope
— the testing and document responsibilities
— the production start condition and the timeline
— the inspection, shipping and buyer responsibilities
— the reorder and change-control terms

A price and a lead time are not a contract. These nine items are the contract. The ninth is the one that decides whether the second order goes smoothly or repeats the whole negotiation.
